entries.note: Became a standard greeting only in the 1870s with the telephone, proposed by [[see:Thomas Edison]]; it varies older hailing calls [[from:hallo]] and [[from:hollo]].
An older call used to hail someone at a distance, such as from ship to ship; it gave [[gave:hello]].
A variant of [[same-root:hallo]] used to get someone's attention from afar; it lies behind [[gave:hello]] and [[gave:hullabaloo]].
Literally means far sound; the first technology for speaking to people far away, which made the hailing word [[see:hello]] a good fit.
The German word for a [[equivalent:telephone]], at least in the past, meaning far speaker.
[[see:Alexander Graham Bell]]'s preferred telephone greeting, used by [[see:Mr Burns]]; the English put an a in front of Dutch [[from:hoi]], learned from rivals at sea.
Wanted [[see:ahoy]] as the telephone greeting but lost out to [[see:Thomas Edison]]'s [[see:hello]].
The Simpsons character who answers the phone with [[see:ahoy]].
A Dutch greeting still used today, the Dutch version of hi, and the source of [[gave:ahoy]].
The better marketer, who proposed [[see:hello]] for the telephone and got manufacturers' booklets to standardise it, ending calls with [[see:that is all]].
Based on [[from:hollo]] and often spelled hollo-ballo, as in Smollett's 1762 novel; it suggests loud noise rather than a simple greeting.
The phrase telephone booklets, influenced by [[see:Thomas Edison]], recommended saying to end a call.
The name for the telephone operators who connected calls, almost all young women, after the [[see:hello]] they said.
The German telephone greeting, one of many languages' versions of [[equivalent:hello]].
The French telephone greeting, borrowed from English [[equivalent:hello]].
The Italian telephone greeting, meaning ready to begin talking; slangy American English pronto, do something quickly, is presumably adapted from it.
Literally means slave, from [[from:schiavo]] and medieval Latin sclavus, as in your obedient servant; now a near-universal hello or goodbye across Europe.
A Shakespearean greeting, used by Hortensio to Katherine in The Taming of the Shrew; it survives as [[gave:wotcher]].
A British greeting, used around London, East Anglia and the Home Counties, from [[from:what cheer]]; said by [[see:Nymphadora Tonks]] in the Harry Potter films.
The Harry Potter character who says [[see:wotcher]], baffling many American viewers.
An East Midlands greeting, made of [[see:ay up]] and [[see:me duck]]; [[see:Angelina Jolie]] used it to introduce [[see:Jack O'Connell]].
The greeting part of [[see:ay up me duck]], said to come from an Old Norse term for watch out, since the area was in the Danelaw.
East Midlands for my dear or my love; men there normally call one another duck too.
Used [[see:ay up me duck]] in front of a crowd to welcome [[see:Jack O'Connell]] on stage.
A local actor from Rob's area who made it in Hollywood; [[see:Angelina Jolie]] introduced him with [[see:ay up me duck]].
Also jumped on the bandwagon of saying [[see:ay up me duck]], though no one knew what it meant.
Jess says [[see:ay up]] evokes what's up or [[see:heads up]].
Jess says [[see:ay up]] evokes [[see:what's up]] or heads up.
A Southern greeting contracted over time from [[from:how do you do]] and how do ye, between the 14th century and the 1720s; much older than [[see:hello]].
A greeting Shakespeare's characters often use, now more associated with the United States and Native American culture.
A Shakespearean greeting used in As You Like It and Hamlet (how now, sweet queen), echoed in [[see:how now brown cow]].
The phrase Rob is reminded of by the Shakespearean greeting [[see:how now]].
A greeting used by a citizen in Richard III, though today it is more likely said, somewhat ironically, to someone departing.
A greeting from Richard III wishing someone a good morning, built on [[from:morrow]]; good morrow was very common before [[see:good morning]].
One of many time-based greetings; it can also be said as a goodbye, which helped [[see:goodbye]] gain its good.
One of the time-based greetings that used to be common.
A time-based greeting that was sometimes shortened to [[gave:good e'en]].
A shortened form of [[from:good evening]].
A German time-based greeting, given to show such greetings are as common there today as they once were in English.
A French time-based greeting, compared with old English ones like [[equivalent:good day]].
An earlier word for morning, dating back to Old English, found in [[gave:give you good tomorrow]].
Means the next morning, built on [[from:morrow]].
Compared with the once very common [[see:give you good tomorrow]].
From Old English [[from:grētan]], to come into contact with; it once also meant seek, find, salute or attack, and goes back to a source meaning to call out.
Now often military, but from Latin [[from:salus]], greetings and good health, whose source is related to the Latin word for [[same-root:safe]].
The source of [[same-root:salute]] is related to the word safe.
Related to [[same-root:salute]] and [[same-root:safe]], so it is really a hope that someone is safe, happy and healthy.
The Thai greeting gesture, hands together and head bowed; it was the standard greeting until the 1940s, and the same bow as [[see:namaste]], from India.
Imposed as the standard Thai greeting by a 1940s dictator's decree; it also means prosperity and shares Sanskrit roots with [[same-root:swastika]].
From a Sanskrit word for prosperity and good luck, shared with [[same-root:sawasdee]]; the symbol is still common in Asia without its Nazi associations.
The form of [[see:sawasdee]] a male speaker uses; men also add khrap to please and thank you.
The form of [[see:sawasdee]] a female speaker uses, whoever she addresses; women also add kha to please and thank you.
Literally I bow to you; the bow is the same one the Thai use in the [[see:wai]], which they got from India.
An Arabic greeting from the same source as Hebrew [[same-root:shalom]]; Jess finds it comforting and friendly.
A Hebrew greeting from the same source as Arabic [[same-root:salam]].
The full Arabic greeting related to [[see:salam]], which Jess finds a comforting sentiment.
Both question and answer, so a whole conversation can be held with it; a shortening of the formal [[from:comment allez-vous]].
The Budweiser advert where the whole conversation is this one word, recalling [[see:ça va]].
The formal version behind [[gave:ça va]], itself said to be short for [[from:comment allez-vous à la selle]].
According to French websites, the source of [[gave:comment allez-vous]], from early medicine judging health by bowel movements; Rob found no English source.
Like English [[see:stool]], both something you sit on and what you pass into the toilet.
Compared with French [[see:selle]]: both mean a seat and a bowel movement.
A fatalistic French farewell, meaning roughly to God, as in I'll never see you again, unlike [[see:au revoir]].
The French goodbye meaning until I see you again, contrasted with the more final [[see:adieu]].
Often taught as the standard Japanese goodbye, but Rob was told it sounds like a final farewell, as if going outside to die.
Like Spanish [[equivalent:adiós]], perhaps a more hopeful God go with you, comparable to [[see:goodbye]].
Interpreted as a hopeful God go with you, like [[see:goodbye]].
Most convincingly short for God be with ye, written in letters as God b w ye; God became good by analogy with [[see:good day]].
Bye wasn't a word before [[from:goodbye]]; bye-bye just references it.
The plural of you, or just a shortened you, at the end of early spellings of [[see:goodbye]].
Once considered too casual by Jess's teachers, though it and [[see:hi]] are older than [[see:hello]] for saluting someone.
Like [[see:hey]], an older term than [[see:hello]] for greeting someone, even from a distance.
What Jess's teachers said to discourage [[see:hey]] as a greeting in favour of [[see:hello]], ironically the younger word.
